name: Thomas Chalmers Statue
address: George Street at Castle Street, Edinburgh
description: A standing bronze of Dr Thomas Chalmers (1780-1847), theologian and reformer who became the first Moderator of the Free Church of Scotland. Sculpted by Sir John Steell and unveiled in 1878, he stands robed as Moderator with a large open Bible on his left forearm, his right hand marking the page. The bronze rises from a stepped red granite plinth carrying a bare inscription: "THOMAS CHALMERS DD DCL BORN 1780 DIED 1847" - no list of achievements, just the facts of a life that reshaped the Church of Scotland.
interesting_fact: Retrace your steps and you've already passed the building where his story peaked. On 18 May 1843, at St Andrew's and St George's Church back along George Street, Chalmers led roughly a third of the ministers at the Church of Scotland's General Assembly out in protest at state interference in church appointments - the "Disruption." Outside, he was cheered through the streets to found the Free Church of Scotland as its first Moderator, a sustentation fund already drawn up to support the hundreds of ministers who had just given up manse and salary. This statue, raised three decades later, put him back on the street where it happened.
source_notes: Sculptor/date/inscription confirmed via trove.scot/Canmore listing record (bronze on stepped red granite plinth, inscribed "THOMAS CHALMERS DD DCL BORN 1780 DIED 1847"). Public-subscription funding for the statue could not be confirmed in sources checked - omitted rather than invented. Disruption date (18 May 1843) and Chalmers's role confirmed via Wikipedia; connects directly to leg 1's "St Andrew's and St George's West Church" landmark, the actual site of the walkout.

name: Walter Scott's House
description: A plain, handsome three-storey Georgian townhouse just off George Street, built for Sir Walter Scott and his family's winter home from 1801 to 1826. It was here, at what he affectionately called "the cabin," that Scott wrote the bulk of the Waverley novels that made him the best-selling author in Europe, working before his day job at the Court of Session even began. Category A listed, the house remains a private residence today, its exterior essentially unchanged since Scott's time.
interesting_fact: In January 1826 Scott's printing and publishing partnerships collapsed under debts of well over £100,000, and rather than declare bankruptcy he spent the rest of his life writing to pay it off - a decision that cost him his health. He recorded leaving Castle Street for the last time in his journal: "This morning I leave No. 39 Castle Street for the last time... So farewell, poor 39." J.M.W. Turner painted the house in 1834, two years after Scott's death, titling the work simply "Former Residence of Walter Scott."
source_notes: Specific novels written at this address are not individually itemised in the sources checked (only that Scott, resident here 1801-1826, published at least one new Waverley novel most years across that span) - description says "the bulk of the Waverley novels" rather than listing titles, to avoid overclaiming. Turner's 1834 painting "Former Residence of Walter Scott" confirmed via Tate.org.uk. Journal quote on leaving the house confirmed via University of Edinburgh library blog.

name: Church of Scotland Offices
description: A big, Scandinavian-flavoured office block built 1909-11 for the United Free Church of Scotland, designed by Edinburgh architect Sydney Mitchell. Its steep double-pitched mansard roof and heavy stonework read closer to Stockholm than to the Georgian street around it. A matching bookshop extension went up next door at 119 George Street in the 1930s, and the complex has held a chapel and staff canteen since it was built. Category A listed, it remains the administrative headquarters of the Church of Scotland.
interesting_fact: The building was finished eighteen years before its own name became accurate. It was built for the United Free Church of Scotland - descended from the Free Church that Thomas Chalmers founded after the 1843 Disruption, whose statue stands a short walk back along this street - and only became genuinely "Church of Scotland offices" when the two churches reunited in 1929, healing a rift that had run for generations. A planned matching extension on the west side was never built, though the church did buy the neighbouring building at 123 George Street.
source_notes: Simplified schism history for length: the 1929 reunion was between the (established) Church of Scotland and the United Free Church of Scotland, which was itself formed in 1900 from the Free Church that Chalmers founded in 1843 and the United Presbyterian Church - description's "descended from the Free Church that Thomas Chalmers founded" is directionally accurate but skips the 1900 intermediate merger.

name: Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel
address: 38 Charlotte Square, Edinburgh (corner of George Street)
description: A row of grand Georgian townhouses at the corner where George Street opens into Charlotte Square, designed by Robert Adam in 1791 as part of his unified palace-front scheme for the square, and reworked in 1810 by his successor as the Crown's Scottish architect, Robert Reid. Two of the houses, Nos 38 and 39, were knocked together to form a hotel in the 1870s, with more of the terrace absorbed over later decades. Long known as the Roxburghe Hotel, it was rebranded in 2019 as the Kimpton Charlotte Square, though the Adam-Reid facade above street level is unchanged.
interesting_fact: The address hides one of the New Town's stranger continuities: architects kept adapting the shell of Adam's 1791 townhouses rather than replacing them, as the building passed from private residence to hotel through several names and refits, including a 1939 remodel that finally opened up the blind ground-floor windows facing the square. Guests today sleep behind the same pilastered facade Adam drew for householders who never imagined a hotel there - and it looks out across the gardens at the domed former church Robert Reid designed after inheriting Adam's unbuilt commission for the opposite side of the square.
source_notes: Formerly the Roxburghe Hotel, rebranded 2019 as Kimpton Charlotte Square (confirmed via multiple 2019 press/travel sources) - Google Places itself now returns "Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel" for this address, not "Roxburghe", confirming the rebrand is reflected in current listings. Robert Adam 1791 / Robert Reid 1810 attribution and 1939 refit details are from a britishlistedbuildings.co.uk search-result excerpt (the page itself 403'd on direct fetch, so not independently re-verified against the primary listing text).

name: Prince Albert Memorial
description: A 30-foot bronze equestrian statue of Prince Albert in Field Marshal's uniform, rearing on a granite pedestal at the centre of Charlotte Square Gardens. Sculpted by Sir John Steell, who won the commission after Albert's sudden death from typhoid in December 1861, it was unveiled by Queen Victoria in person on 17 August 1876 - Steell was knighted by the Queen on the spot. Four bronze figure groups ring the base, each by a different sculptor: William Brodie's Nobility, Clark Stanton's Army and Navy, and D.W. Stevenson's Labour and Science and Learning.
interesting_fact: It took Victoria fifteen years to unveil a monument to her own husband, by which point several other Albert memorials already stood elsewhere in Britain. The horse was cast from a single piece with no visible joins, reckoned a technical feat at the time. And the garden it stands in is still private: unlike St Andrew Square at the other end of this walk, opened to the public in 2008, Charlotte Square Gardens remain locked and keyholder-only, open to everyone only a handful of days a year - so the statue is usually viewed through railings, not up close.
source_notes: Competition year for the commission is given as both 1863 and 1865 across sources checked - description avoids stating a specific year, using only Albert's death (Dec 1861) and the well-corroborated unveiling date (17 Aug 1876). Four corner-figure sculptor attributions (Brodie/Nobility, Stanton/Army and Navy, D.W. Stevenson/Labour and Science & Learning) come from one source, not cross-checked against a second. Charlotte Square Gardens confirmed still private and keyholder-only today (not just historically) via multiple current sources - contrasted with St Andrew Square's 2008 public opening, per leg 1 sourcing.

name: West Register House
description: A great domed building closing the west side of Charlotte Square, built 1811-14 as St George's Church to a design by Robert Reid, reworking an earlier scheme for the same site that Robert Adam had drawn up before his death in 1792. The foundation stone was laid on 14 May 1811, and the church opened on 5 June 1814 with seating for around 1,600 worshippers beneath a green copper dome and gilt cupola rising some 160 feet, deliberately styled to echo St Paul's Cathedral in London. Its pulpit, carved in Spanish mahogany, stood a full 20 feet high.
interesting_fact: The £18,000 budget nearly doubled to £33,000 by completion - not the last time this building would be rebuilt from within. St George's closed as a congregation in 1964, merging with St Andrew's Church further along George Street (where Chalmers led the 1843 Disruption), and by 1970 the sacred interior had been gutted and replaced with five storeys of fireproof archive stacks. It reopened as West Register House, one of the two homes of the National Records of Scotland, still holding some of the nation's oldest legal documents under the dome once built for hymn-singing.
source_notes: Distance flag: sits on the far (west) side of Charlotte Square, roughly 100-115m from Bute House/Georgian House rather than directly alongside the George-Street-to-Bute-House path itself - included anyway as the dominant, unmissable building forming the whole west side of the square, clearly visible across the gardens from the route (per the leg brief's "roughly 100m" being a guideline, not a hard cutoff). The 1964 merger partner, "St Andrew's and St George's" church at 13 George Street, is leg 1's landmark #11 (that church later added "West" to its own name to distinguish from a separate congregation - not covered here for length).

name: The Georgian House
description: A National Trust for Scotland museum recreating a New Town townhouse at the height of Georgian fashion, in a house built in 1796 for John Lamont, 18th Chief of Clan Lamont, who lived here until 1815. From 1889 it was home to theologian Rev Alexander Whyte, minister of nearby Free St George's, and his wife Jane, who raised eight children within it. The Marquess of Bute acquired the house in 1927; on the 5th Marquess's death in 1956, Nos 5, 6 and 7 passed to the National Trust in part settlement of death duties, restored and opened to the public in 1975.
interesting_fact: For decades before it became a museum, No.7 served as an antique dealer's showroom - the very trade the house now exists to interpret, minus the historical accuracy. Lamont bought the newly built house for a little over £1,800 and sold it twenty years later for £3,000, trying and failing to offset debts that helped push his clan's finances into decline. The house stands directly next to No.6, Bute House, official residence of Scotland's First Minister since 1999 - a debt-ridden chief's townhouse sharing a garden wall with the seat of the devolved Scottish government.
source_notes: Death-duties/Land Fund mechanism by which Nos 5-7 passed to NTS in 1956/1966 is repeated across several tourism sources but not traced to a primary NTS record. Antique-dealer-showroom detail (pre-1973) and Lamont's purchase/resale prices confirmed via NTS and Undiscovered Scotland sources.
